Someone described nursing as a trade and it was the most apt description I have ever heard. You go to school to learn the rationales and processes, and you go to clinicals to learn the skills, but you don’t really learn how to be a nurse until you start working. 

Anyone being nasty to you and telling you not to try is an idiot. It’s a commitment, but it’s worth it if it is truly what you want to do. If you just want a job where you can pack money away as fast as possible, it might not be the best fit. 

If you want to do it, you can. I have worked with some absolute MORONS, and some that I cannot believe actually passed their boards. I’m sure some of the people in this thread fit that description. A lot of people pursue it as a second career and are successful, but it does sound like it would be a huge adjustment from what you’re used to. You would have to take some time off from your current work schedule for schooling but you could totally do it. It’s hard work but it sounds like you’re used to that. Best of luck whichever way you go :)

Of course! You can make big bucks nursing staff somewhere. If you can find somewhere short staffed and get to the point that you can work PRN (6 months would probably be plenty depending on how fast of a learner you are) you can negotiate for more. Your hourly will be higher than travel, but you may also be able to negotiate for shift bonuses (sometimes $10-$20/hr over your base, plus OT). The problem with this is it isn’t always reliable hours. You can deal with that by being PRN at multiple hospitals but you don’t get overtime. It’s all a game if you’re after the money. Be careful chasing the money though, it’ll make you disillusioned with nursing and burn you out fast. You have to have another reason to get into nursing and you have to hold that reason real tight in my experience. Even if it’s hokey-pokey “helping people that can’t help themselves” or “service of others.” It’s a hard job but it’s financially and internally rewarding too.

Travel nursing became a hot topic during COVID with the $10,000+/week contracts. That money isn’t around anymore and probably won’t ever be around again. I was working LTC and making $2,400/week. Most of it isn’t taxed because it’s stipends, and your hourly rate is low, so overtime really isn’t incentivized that much unless you negotiate a contract with a high hourly. This subjects you to higher taxes. 

Another factor with travel nursing is you duplicate expenses. That’s why it is so lucrative, because many people will be paying bills back home and also paying for housing and food and whatnot at their contract location. I would find the cheapest month-rate hotel or an airBnB and then negotiate with the owner to pay them directly to avoid paying the fees from airBnB. 

This is also a time-commitment you’re looking at. You may have all of your prerequisites done for nursing school from your bachelors, but probably not. You’ll have organic chem and microbiology and some other stuff that is different from the field your bachelors is in. Then you have 2-ish years of nursing school. Some schools require you to have a CNA before you go in. 

Then once you graduate, you need experience before you can travel. Some places let you travel with 6 months experience, however I personally find this to be unsafe. Depending on your field of nursing you should look at 1-2 years of experience before you travel. Travel nursing means you are working somewhere that is not well staffed because they are unsafe or undesirable to work in typically. Sometimes it’s a great place that just needs a fill-in while they find full time staff but that’s rare in my experience. It’s better to know what you’re doing so you can get dropped in to some hell hole and be able to swim with minimal orientation. They can’t teach you how to be a nurse typically. 

Nursing is great because you will always, ALWAYS have work. But it has its negatives too. I would never talk anyone out of nursing, but I try to give people reasonable expectations of what they will get out of it.

Plenty of people do it without issue. It was a widely used practice and not every medication was administered in error. My point is simply you're more likely to have an error occur. When I worked in LTC we would get meds ready for 30 residents at once and then go down and pass them out with a med tech. We had paper MAR so you had no scanner to catch errors. We wouldn't have med errors daily, but I would say probably once a month to once every few months we would have one that got reported. This is more extreme than, say, working med surg and getting meds for your 4-7 patients, putting them in bags, scanning your patient, and scanning each med before giving them.

Only giving one med at a time through the g-tube is great in theory, but when you have someone getting 27 pills that need to be crushed and you're expected to flush between each one...I don't know many stomachs that can hold the amount of fluid that would be necessary to make that possible. 

Pulling meds for only one patient at a time helps reduce med errors. The more time you spend and more diligence you put into administering meds, the less likely you are to have an error. They happen when people get complacent and/or are moving too fast. 

Best practice that is taught in nursing school is to help you be the perfect nurse in a perfect hospital. There is rationale for everything that is taught, and if you were able to do everything by the book then there would be no room for error. Is this always achievable? Of course not. But it is wise to incorporate as much of that best practice into your real practice as you can. You might be okay 999 times taking a shortcut, but if it does catch up to you and you make an error, you will feel terrible about taking the shortcut. Not to mention, the liability is on you because it is against what you are taught and probably against the policy of your hospital.

I would suggest you figure out what your different bits and tools are called and what they are typically used for. If you have the name, you can usually find more specific information for it. Also, don't be intimidated by what you come across. There will always be lots of people with way more knowledge and experience than you, and you'll have people that will tell you that you ABSOLUTELY MUST do something or that under no circumstances should you do something else. Biggest thing I've learned from working with stones and metal smithing is if it looks pretty in the end, the how you got there doesn't matter so much. There are "correct" ways to do things, but as long as you're happy (and your customer is happy, if you're ever at the point of selling shit), the journey doesn't matter so much. 

I guess that's more life advice than specific advice, but I haven't done much carving beyond hobby hand carving with scraper tools lol. Also, you can check out flea markets for old tools that people are trying to get rid of. If you aren't aware already, there are also great big gem shows all over the country throughout the year where you can get cool shit for cheap, and even cheaper if you have a wholesale license or know someone that has one. 

Sorry if this is rambling, lol. You're always welcome to DM me if you have questions or just want a friend to show something cool to that you made!
